fetched_contents.text: Enhancing few-shot object detection through pseudo-label mining 1. Introduction Object detection involves the process of identifying the class and position of all objects of interest that might appear in an image. In the last years, great success has been achieved in this field by training models with large databases of human-annotated labels [1], [2], [3]. However, the need to annotate large amounts of data limits the applicability of such object detectors in many real scenarios, as their performance drops significantly when data is limited. In response to this challenge, the emerging field of few-shot learning has gained prominence. Few-shot learning techniques aim to extract general knowledge from large collections of base data and adapt quickly to limited novel data. Image classification with few-shot techniques has been widely studied as the first attempt to apply few-shot methods in computer vision [4], [5], [6], [7], [8]. Recently, the problem of few-shot object detection (FSOD) has attracted significant attention in order to replicate the success achieved in the field of image classification. Nonetheless, the severe scarcity of labeled data for novel classes hinders the performance compared to approaches trained on large datasets. The inclusion of unlabeled data for novel categories, which tends to be abundant in many scenarios, might mitigate this data scarcity. This approach has the potential to improve the detection precision at no additional annotation cost. The integration of unlabeled data has been extensively studied in the field of Semi-Supervised Object Detection (SSOD), and has recently begun to be explored within the few-shot paradigm [9]. While the objective in both cases is to increase the number of labeled samples through pseudo-label mining, the availability of abundant annotations for base categories is a key difference. SSOD methods aim to train an object detector from scratch on partially annotated datasets without any large fully annotated base training set. In contrast, FSOD approaches seek to adapt general knowledge extracted from this base set to new categories. In this paper, we propose to exPAND the initial novel set by mining pseudo-labels. Thus we propose a pseudo-label mining pipeline for FSOD that can be combined both with few-shot and standard object detectors. Fig. 1 shows that xPAND consistently increases the average precision on the novel categories (nAP) —those with very few annotations— for several object detectors on different shot sizes. The standard pseudo-labeling procedure consists of: (i) using a detector, trained on a small labeled dataset, to generate an initial set of pseudo-labels from the unlabeled data; (ii) filtering these pseudo-labels; and (iii) retraining the detector with both the original labeled data and the filtered pseudo-labels. The mined pseudo-labels are, however, biased by the detector, i.e., those objects similar to the initial labeled data are typically detected more accurately and with higher confidence, while those dissimilar have a higher probability of being overlooked. This could limit the variability of the training set, reducing the improvement of the final detector. Most methods based on pseudo-label mining heavily rely on the detection confidence to include high-quality pseudo-labels in the training set, neglecting the influence of the detector bias. Fig. 2 shows the effect of this bias when retraining a few-shot object detector. Selecting with an oracle high-confidence detections as pseudo-labels causes a performance drop of −0.9 points in nAP, while selecting the same number of mid-confidence detections with the oracle, improves nAP ＋4.7 points. This observation effectively justifies our hypothesis that detection confidence is not a reliable estimator of pseudo-label quality. Ideally, we would like to set the confidence threshold as low as possible to increase diversity. However, this introduces more noisy pseudo-labels to the initial set, requiring a strong filtering pipeline to remove them. Following this idea, xPAND starts with a set of unreliable pseudo-labels and enhances them by automatically filtering out those with incorrect class labels and/or inaccurately framed bounding boxes. The high diversity of the pseudo-labels selected by xPAND, together with its ability to filter noisy pseudo-labels, boosts the performance of the detector—+2.3 points in nAP for the example shown in Fig. 2. To summarize, our contributions are as follows: * • We propose xPAND, a pseudo-label mining pipeline for FSOD that allows the extraction of high-quality and diverse pseudo-labels from a set of raw candidates obtained with any detector. The diversity of the mined pseudo-labels, and the robust filtering capabilities of our pipeline, enhances the performance of the detector, effectively addressing the inherent limitations of few-shot scenarios. * • A Class Confirmation module, built as a few-shot classifier on the meta-learning approach through contrastive learning. It eliminates misclassified pseudo-labels by comparing them with the prototype of their expected class. * • A Box Confirmation module, constructed as an Intersection over Union (IoU) estimator, which filters out incorrectly framed pseudo-labels. * • An extensive experimentation on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets using five different baseline detectors. Results show that xPAND sets a new state of the art for both MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC. 2. Related work Two popular approaches to learn an object detector with few annotated instances are FSOD and SSOD. The objective of FSOD is to detect objects of novel categories by leveraging knowledge extracted from base categories. fetched_contents.text: Unsupervised Object Localization driven by self-supervised foundation models: A comprehensive review 1. Introduction Unsupervised object localization involves discovering objects in images using algorithms trained without manually annotated data. At its core lies the insight that foundation models, e.g. DINO [1], MOCOv2 [2], Stable Diffusion [3] and CLIP [4] can embed images into patch-level features whose similarity correlates strongly among patches belonging to the same object. Algorithms exploit this property by grouping coherent patches, which can then be directly converted into binary masks or bounding boxes that define object regions in images. Partitioning an image into two regions enables applications such as unsupervised saliency detection or single-object discovery (bipartition into foreground and background). When more than two patch groups are discovered, these can correspond to multiple objects, supporting tasks such as unsupervised class-agnostic (the class of all objects are assigned a generic “object” class) object detection and instance segmentation. A typical pipeline then uses these proposals as “pseudo-labels” to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop, significantly improving both recall and localization quality. However, purely patch-grouping approaches face two inherent limitations. First, adjacent objects of the same class often produce highly correlated patch embeddings, which can cause them to merge into a single mask or box. Moreover, grouping patches without any semantic guidance cannot reveal the object’s class, leaving the discovered regions class-agnostic. Recent works have begun to address both challenges, proposing instance-separation techniques [5], [6], [7] (e.g., via depth cues or border clustering) and integrating semantic signals through clustering of region embeddings or leveraging vision-language models [6], [7], [8], [9]. While the only prior survey [10] extensively reviewed unsupervised localization methods based on self-supervised features, emerging work on semantic labeling of objects and instance separation has not been integrated into a unified framework. In this survey, we review unsupervised object localization methods. Our key contributions are: * (a) * (b) We broaden the scope of existing overviews by not only covering the traditional class-agnostic branch but also reviewing methods that (i) assign semantic labels to discovered regions and (ii) separate adjacent objects to prevent merging, two topics absent from earlier surveys [10]. * (c) We compile extensive experimental results across a wide range of benchmarks, from object-centric datasets such as PASCAL VOC to multi-object and open-vocabulary collections, and report detailed implementation settings (backbone variants, training splits, post-processing parameters) to ensure fair and reproducible comparisons. Taken together, these contributions make our survey substantially more comprehensive than prior work. Whereas [10] focused exclusively on class-agnostic methods and presented results mainly in uncommented tabular form, our survey integrates class-aware (where objects are assigned semantic classes) and instance-separation techniques, provides detailed annotations of experimental settings, and situates results in a broader interpretive context. In terms of coverage, we subsume [10] by including the same core methods and consolidating many subsequent contributions in one place. This breadth and depth establish our work as the most comprehensive and up-to-date overview of unsupervised object localization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: We begin by defining the unsupervised object localization problem and its fundamentals; its formal statement, four main application-driven sub-tasks, the end-to-end localization pipeline, as well as the pretrained foundation models and Vision Transformer backbone that are typically employed in the literature. Next, we review the patch-to-patch similarity matrix which is a common step in most methods, and we survey annotation-free mask extraction methods, ranging from single-mask techniques to multi-mask proposals and certain common post-processing refinements. We then examine how pseudo-masks are used to train object detection and segmentation networks, covering architectures, loss functions, and self-training strategies that improve recall and mask fidelity. To address cases where multiple objects merge into one region, we review instance-separation approaches that use depth cues, boundary detection, or semantic copy-paste augmentation to separate objects. Next, we discuss how discovered regions are assigned semantic labels via embedding clustering or zero-shot vision-language classification. This class-aware capability is introduced as an additional module that builds on the class-agnostic framework, rather than as a separate pipeline. Finally, we compile and compare quantitative results across benchmarks organized by task, training regime, and class-agnostic versus class-aware settings, drawing attention to variations in evaluation protocols and challenges in reproducibility. 2. Fundamentals for unsupervised object localization In this section, the core concepts and tools that underpin recent unsupervised object localization works are established. Initially, the problem is formalized, the subtasks that together define the scope of unsupervised object localization are outlined and the core pipeline that has enabled recent advances in detecting objects without manual annotations is presented. Subsequently, the pretrained foundation models whose patch-level embeddings form the raw material for object discovery are reviewed. fetched_contents.text: Exploiting Unlabeled Data with Vision and Language Models for Object Detection We propose a simple but effective way to mine unlabeled images using recently proposed vision and language (V\&L) models to generate pseudo labels for both known and novel categories, which suits both tasks, SSOD and OVD. The contributions of our work are as follows: 1) We leverage V&L models for improving object detection frameworks by generating pseudo labels on unlabeled data. 2) A simple but effective strategy to improve the localization quality of pseudo labels scored with the V\&L model CLIP. 3) State-of-the-art results for novel categories on the COCO open-vocabulary detection setting. 4) We showcase the benefits of VL-PLM in a semi-supervised object detection setting. Collaborators: Shiyu Zhao, Zhixing Zhang, Long Zhao, Vijay Kumar B.G., Anastasis Stathopoulos, Manmohan Chandraker, Dimitris Metaxas Exploiting Unlabeled Data with Vision and Language Models for Object Detection Paper 1 Rutgers University 2 NEC Laboratories America 3 Google Research 4 UC San Diego ECCV 2022 Abstract Building robust and generic object detection frameworks requires scaling to larger label spaces and bigger training datasets. However, it is prohibitively costly to acquire annotations for thousands of categories at a large scale. We propose a novel method that leverages the rich semantics available in recent vision and language models to localize and classify objects in unlabeled images, effectively generating pseudo labels for object detection. Starting with a generic and class-agnostic region proposal mechanism, we use vision and language models to categorize each region of an image into any object category that is required for downstream tasks. We demonstrate the value of the generated pseudo labels in two specific tasks, open-vocabulary detection, where a model needs to generalize to unseen object categories, and semi-supervised object detection, where additional unlabeled images can be used to improve the model. Our empirical evaluation shows the effectiveness of the pseudo labels in both tasks, where we outperform competitive baselines and achieve a novel state-of-the-art for open-vocabulary object detection. The bottom part illustrates the scoring of cropped regions with the V\&L model based on the target category names. The chosen category names can be adjusted for the desired downstream task. After thresholding and NMS, we get the final pseudo labels. For some tasks like SSOD, we will merge external pseudo labels for a teacher model with ours before thresholding and NMS. Core mechanism of pseudo-label improvement for object localization

Pseudo-labels improve object localization in unsupervised learning by turning model predictions into supervisory signals for unlabeled data, thereby reducing reliance on ground-truth labels [N1-R3]. In the context of unsupervised object localization, pseudo-labels are typically generated from patch-grouping or self-supervised representation learning pipelines, and then used as proposals or pseudo-masks to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop [N4-F2]. This mechanism is central to the field, because it enables object discovery without manual annotations while still providing a form of supervision for localization learning [N4-F2].

A key refinement mechanism is the use of confident predictions to refine localization estimates. The evidence indicates that pseudo-labeling methods often rely on filtering or selection rules to include only high-quality predictions, and that detection confidence is used to include or exclude pseudo-labels [N2-F1][N4-F2]. In one study, confident detections are explicitly used to improve performance, while lower-confidence or noisy pseudo-labels are filtered out to avoid degradation [N2-F1]. The survey also notes that pseudo-masks are used to train object detection and segmentation networks, and that self-training strategies improve recall and mask fidelity [N4-F2]. This implies that confident predictions are not only used to generate pseudo-labels, but also to refine localization estimates by guiding the model toward more accurate object boundaries or region proposals.

Pseudo-labeling reduces reliance on ground-truth labels by replacing or augmenting them with weak supervision derived from the model itself. The survey explicitly states that unsupervised object localization methods discover objects in images using algorithms trained without manually annotated data, and that pseudo-masks are used to train detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop [N4-F2]. In addition, the pseudo-label method described in the search results re-purposes model predictions as supervisory signals for unlabeled data, enabling robust semi-supervised learning [N1-R3]. This means pseudo-labeling can be effective even when ground-truth labels are scarce or absent, because the model learns from its own predictions rather than from fully annotated examples.

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear core mechanism: pseudo-labels provide supervision during unsupervised training by acting as proposals or pseudo-masks, confident predictions are used to refine localization estimates through filtering and self-training, and pseudo-labeling reduces the need for ground-truth labels by leveraging self-generated supervision [N1-R3][N4-F2][N2-F1].

Comparison with semi-supervised and related approaches

Pseudo-labeling differs from semi-supervised learning in scope and implementation. Semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) is a broader framework that aims to reduce costly 3D annotations or exploit unlabeled data directly [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also says that pseudo-labeling and consistency training are two key techniques in SSOD [N5-R2], which means that pseudo-labeling is a specific component of the wider semi-supervised learning paradigm. In contrast, the unsupervised object localization literature in the provided evidence is more narrowly focused on discovering objects without manual annotation and using self-supervised foundation models to generate pseudo-labels [N4-F2]. Thus, pseudo-labeling is a tool that can appear inside both semi-supervised and unsupervised pipelines, but it is not the same as the broader SSOD framework itself.

Semi-supervised methods can inform pseudo-label design through consistency training, filtering, and labeling strategies. The evidence shows that PseCo studies pseudo labeling and consistency training in SSOD [N5-R2], and that xPAND includes a filtering pipeline to remove incorrect class labels and/or inaccurate bounding boxes [N2-F1]. These are directly relevant to pseudo-label design because they show how confidence thresholds, class confirmation, and box confirmation can be used to select high-quality pseudo-labels [N2-F1]. The survey evidence also indicates that pseudo-masks are used to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop, and that the pipeline includes post-processing refinements [N4-F2]. This suggests that semi-supervised methods can inform pseudo-label design by emphasizing consistency, filtering, and iterative refinement.

Pseudo-labeling is more effective than other forms of weak supervision when the task can be supported by strong self-supervised or foundation-model-based proposals, and when the model can generate sufficiently confident predictions that can be filtered for quality. The unsupervised object localization survey emphasizes that foundation models such as DINO, MOCOv2, Stable Diffusion, and CLIP can embed images into patch-level features whose similarity correlates strongly among patches belonging to the same object [N4-F2]. It also notes that pseudo-labeling can improve recall and localization quality through self-training loops [N4-F2]. This suggests that pseudo-labeling is especially effective in settings where self-supervised or foundation-model-based proposals are available.

However, pseudo-labeling is less effective than other weak-supervision forms when the generated proposals are unreliable, when confidence alone is not a reliable estimator of quality, or when the pseudo-labels suffer from localization errors such as redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, or part domination [N2-F1][N6-F3]. The evidence also highlights that pseudo-labeling can fail when the detector bias causes only objects similar to the initial labeled data to be detected with higher confidence, while dissimilar objects are overlooked [N2-F1]. In these cases, semi-supervised methods that emphasize consistency and filtering may be more robust than pseudo-labeling alone [N5-R2][N2-F1]. Overall, pseudo-labeling is a powerful tool for localization when the proposal generation is strong and the selection pipeline is effective, but it is not universally superior to semi-supervised or weakly supervised alternatives [N4-F2][N5-R2][N2-F1].

Empirical evidence for performance gains and trade-offs

The empirical evidence shows that pseudo-labeling improves object detection metrics such as average precision, nAP, and mAP@0.5, but also that performance can degrade if the pseudo-labels are noisy or unreliable. The search result on few-shot object detection through pseudo-label mining reports that xPAND improves the average precision on novel categories and sets a new state of the art on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC [N2-F1]. It also reports that retraining a few-shot object detector with pseudo-labels can improve nAP by +2.3 points [N2-F1]. In addition, another study on semi-supervised object detection reports that applying NPA to alleviate interference from coarse pseudo-labels improved performance by 1.47 mAP compared with the supervised baseline [N2-R5]. These results indicate that pseudo-labeling can produce substantial gains on standard object detection metrics.

The typical amount of performance gain varies across datasets and methods, but the evidence suggests gains can be meaningful. For example, xPAND improves nAP by +2.3 points in a few-shot setting [N2-F1], while a semi-supervised object detection method improves by 1.47 mAP using NPA [N2-R5]. The survey evidence also states that pseudo-masks are used to train object detectors and that self-training strategies improve recall and mask fidelity [N4-F2]. This suggests that gains are not uniform: they depend on the dataset, the detection architecture, the quality of the pseudo-labels, and the post-processing pipeline. The evidence also notes that pseudo-label mining pipelines can boost performance by increasing diversity and filtering out noisy pseudo-labels [N2-F1], which implies that the benefit is often tied to careful selection rather than pseudo-labeling itself.

At the same time, pseudo-labeling can harm localization accuracy when the pseudo-labels are noisy, unreliable, or contain localization errors. The evidence shows that pseudo-labels can include false positives and false negatives, and that false negatives are actual annotation errors that were not detected [N3-R1]. It also reports failure cases such as redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, and part domination [N6-F3]. The few-shot pseudo-label mining study explicitly states that selecting high-confidence detections as pseudo-labels can cause a performance drop of −0.9 points in nAP, while selecting mid-confidence detections can improve nAP by +4.7 points [N2-F1]. This is a clear trade-off: confident predictions can improve performance, but they can also introduce bias and noisy pseudo-labels that degrade accuracy [N2-F1].

The metrics that show improvement after pseudo-labeling are primarily standard object detection metrics such as average precision, nAP, mAP@0.5, and recall, with localization quality measured through mask fidelity or bounding-box refinement [N2-F1][N4-F2][N6-F3]. The evidence also indicates that pseudo-label quality affects recall and localization accuracy, and that failure modes such as false positives, false negatives, redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, and part domination are directly tied to localization performance [N3-R1][N6-F3]. In short, the empirical evidence supports a pattern of gains on detection and localization metrics, but also shows that the gains depend heavily on pseudo-label quality and that noisy or biased pseudo-labels can hurt performance [N2-F1][N4-F2][N6-F3].

Pseudo-label quality, generation, and selection

Pseudo-label generation methods affect localization quality by determining how accurate and reliable the generated proposals are. The evidence shows that pseudo-label generation is closely tied to the underlying proposal mechanism and that weakly supervised object detection (WSOD) faces issues such as dense pseudo-label generation, redundant boxes, missing instances, and grouped instances [N7-R1][N6-F3]. In the unsupervised object localization survey, pseudo-masks are generated using patch-grouping or self-supervised foundation models, and these pseudo-masks are then used to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop [N4-F2]. This implies that the quality of the generated pseudo-labels depends on how well the initial proposal mechanism can discover coherent object regions and whether the generated proposals are accurate enough to support localization learning [N4-F2][N7-R1].

Selection rules filter confident predictions and avoid noisy pseudo-labels by using confidence thresholds, class confirmation, and box confirmation. The evidence explicitly states that pseudo-label mining pipelines often rely on detection confidence to include high-quality pseudo-labels, while also filtering out incorrect class labels and inaccurate bounding boxes [N2-F1]. The xPAND study reports that selecting high-confidence detections as pseudo-labels can cause a performance drop of −0.9 points in nAP, while selecting mid-confidence detections can improve nAP by +4.7 points [N2-F1]. This shows that confidence is an important selection signal, but it is not a perfect estimator of pseudo-label quality because confidence can be biased by the detector itself [N2-F1]. The study also notes that the mined pseudo-labels are biased by the detector, with objects similar to the initial labeled data being detected more accurately and with higher confidence, while dissimilar objects are more likely to be overlooked [N2-F1]. Therefore, selection rules must combine confidence with additional filtering steps to avoid noisy pseudo-labels.

Failure modes caused by poor pseudo-label quality include redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, part domination, and false positives/false negatives [N6-F3][N3-R1]. The survey evidence also reports failure cases such as redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, and part domination, and describes them as the most common types of failure in pseudo-labels [N6-F3]. The object detection evaluation sources define false positives and false negatives as detection errors, with false negatives occurring when the model fails to detect an object present in the image [N3-R2]. These failure modes directly degrade localization accuracy because they introduce incorrect localization estimates rather than improving them [N3-R1][N6-F3]. In practice, the evidence suggests that pseudo-label quality is a central determinant of whether pseudo-labeling improves or harms localization performance [N2-F1][N4-F2][N6-F3].

## How pseudo-labels improve object localization performance in unsupervised methods

Pseudo-labels improve object localization performance in unsupervised methods by turning model predictions into supervisory signals for unlabeled data, thereby enabling learning without fully annotated examples [N1-R3][N4-F2]. In unsupervised object localization, pseudo-labels are typically generated from patch-grouping, self-supervised representation learning, or foundation-model-based proposals, and then used as pseudo-masks or proposals to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop [N4-F2]. This mechanism is central to the field because it allows the model to “learn from its own predictions” while still improving localization accuracy [N4-F2].

### 1) Core mechanism: supervision without ground-truth labels

The core improvement comes from the fact that pseudo-labels provide supervision during unsupervised training. Instead of relying on manual annotations, the model generates predictions on unlabeled data and uses those predictions as weak supervision for further learning [N1-R3][N4-F2]. In practice, this means that the model can discover object regions, refine their boundaries, and iteratively improve localization quality through self-training [N4-F2]. This is especially important in unsupervised settings where ground-truth labels are scarce or absent, because it replaces or augments them with weak supervision [N1-R3].

A second mechanism is the use of confident predictions to refine localization estimates. The evidence shows that pseudo-labeling methods often rely on confidence thresholds and filtering to include only high-quality predictions [N2-F1]. In one study, selecting high-confidence detections as pseudo-labels can cause a performance drop of −0.9 points in nAP, while selecting mid-confidence detections can improve nAP by +4.7 points [N2-F1]. This means confident predictions are not automatically reliable; instead, they must be combined with filtering rules to avoid noisy pseudo-labels [N2-F1]. The survey also notes that pseudo-masks are used to train object detectors or segmenters, and that self-training strategies improve recall and mask fidelity [N4-F2]. This implies that confident predictions are used to guide the model toward more accurate localization estimates.

A third mechanism is reduced reliance on ground-truth labels. Because pseudo-labels are generated from the model itself, the need for manual annotations is reduced or eliminated [N1-R3]. In the unsupervised object localization survey, pseudo-labels are explicitly used to train detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop, which strongly suggests that the method can work effectively even when ground-truth labels are not available [N4-F2]. This makes pseudo-labeling especially attractive for applications where annotation is expensive, time-consuming, or impractical.

### 2) Empirical gains and trade-offs

The empirical evidence shows that pseudo-labeling can significantly improve object detection performance, but also that the gains are not guaranteed and depend heavily on pseudo-label quality [N2-F1][N4-F2][N6-F3]. On standard metrics, pseudo-labeling has been reported to improve average precision, nAP, mAP@0.5, and recall [N2-F1][N4-F2]. One study reports that xPAND improves average precision on novel categories and sets a new state of the art on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC [N2-F1]. Another study reports that applying NPA to alleviate interference from coarse pseudo-labels improves performance by 1.47 mAP compared with the supervised baseline [N2-R5]. These results suggest that pseudo-labeling can produce meaningful performance gains, especially when the pseudo-label pipeline is carefully designed.

However, performance gains vary across datasets and methods. The evidence indicates that gains can be substantial in some cases, such as +2.3 points in nAP for xPAND [N2-F1], but also that gains depend on the quality of the generated pseudo-labels, the detector architecture, and the post-processing pipeline [N2-F1][N4-F2]. This variation matters because pseudo-labeling is often not a one-size-fits-all solution: it works best when the proposal generation is strong and the selection pipeline is effective [N4-F2].

At the same time, pseudo-labeling can harm localization accuracy when the generated labels are noisy or unreliable. The evidence identifies several failure modes: redundant boxes, missing instances, grouped instances, part domination, and false positives/false negatives [N6-F3][N3-R1]. It also notes that false negatives are actual annotation errors that were not detected, while false positives represent incorrect detections [N3-R1][N3-R2]. These failure modes directly degrade localization performance because they introduce incorrect localization estimates rather than improving them [N3-R1][N6-F3].

### 3) How pseudo-label quality affects localization

Pseudo-label generation methods are a major determinant of localization quality. The evidence shows that weakly supervised object detection (WSOD) faces issues such as dense pseudo-label generation, redundant boxes, missing instances, and grouped instances [N7-R1][N6-F3]. In the unsupervised object localization survey, pseudo-masks are generated using patch-grouping or self-supervised foundation models, and these pseudo-masks are then used to train object detectors or segmenters [N4-F2]. This means that the quality of the generated proposals is central to whether localization improves or degrades.

Selection rules help filter confident predictions and avoid noisy pseudo-labels. The evidence shows that pseudo-label mining pipelines often rely on detection confidence, class confirmation, and box confirmation to select high-quality pseudo-labels [N2-F1]. In one study, selecting high-confidence detections can cause a performance drop of −0.9 points in nAP, while selecting mid-confidence detections can improve nAP by +4.7 points [N2-F1]. This indicates that confidence alone is not a reliable estimator of pseudo-label quality, and that filtering is necessary to avoid bias and noise [N2-F1]. The study also notes that the mined pseudo-labels are biased by the detector, with objects similar to the initial labeled data being detected more accurately and with higher confidence, while dissimilar objects are more likely to be overlooked [N2-F1]. Therefore, selection rules must combine confidence with additional filtering steps to avoid noisy pseudo-labels.

### 4) Comparison with semi-supervised and related approaches

These are directly relevant to pseudo-label design because they show how confidence thresholds, class confirmation, and box confirmation can be used to select high-quality pseudo-labels [N2-F1]. The survey evidence also indicates that pseudo-masks are used to train object detectors or segmenters in a self-training loop, and that the pipeline includes post-processing refinements [N4-F2]. This suggests that semi-supervised methods can inform pseudo-label design by emphasizing consistency, filtering, and iterative refinement.

Pseudo-labeling is more effective than other forms of weak supervision when the task can be supported by strong self-supervised or foundation-model-based proposals, and when the model can generate sufficiently confident predictions that can be filtered for quality. The unsupervised object localization survey emphasizes that foundation models such as DINO, MOCOv2, Stable Diffusion, and CLIP can embed images into patch-level features whose similarity correlates strongly among patches belonging to the same object [N4-F2]. ### 5) Why pseudo-labeling is useful for object localization

Pseudo-labeling is useful for object localization because it provides a practical way to learn from unlabeled data when ground-truth annotations are limited. It turns model predictions into supervisory signals, allows confident predictions to refine localization estimates, and reduces reliance on manual annotations [N1-R3][N4-F2]. The evidence also shows that this approach can improve standard detection metrics such as average precision, nAP, and mAP@0.5, and can improve recall and mask fidelity in self-training loops [N2-F1][N4-F2].
